planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in consistently moist to seasonally flooded, acidic soil in partial shade; pondspice colonizes the shaded margins of cypress ponds, Carolina bays, and steephead-adjacent seepage pools and tolerates standing water for weeks at a time.

directions: Pondspice is a thicket-forming deciduous shrub of the laurel family found in shallow, seasonally flooded depressions scattered through the Coastal Plain from Maryland to the Florida Panhandle, including the still pools that form where steephead ravine streams widen near pond and swamp margins. Clusters of tiny, chartreuse-yellow flowers open directly on bare twigs in very early spring, well before the narrow, willow-like leaves emerge, followed later by small shiny red drupes that persist into fall. It spreads slowly by root suckers to form loose colonies and is naturally adapted to prolonged inundation alternating with drier summer spells, making it a good choice for the wet edge of a rain garden or pond. Because the species is state-listed as endangered in Florida and threatened in Georgia, and increasingly threatened by laurel wilt disease, source only nursery-propagated plants from licensed growers rather than wild-collected material.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in fall or early spring in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; Carolina basswood establishes readily on the cool, north-facing slopes of ravines and bluffs where the canopy filters direct sun.

directions: Carolina basswood is the southern coastal plain counterpart of American basswood, forming part of the rich, mesic canopy of steephead ravine slopes and bluff forests across the Florida Panhandle, southern Georgia, and Alabama alongside beech and southern magnolia. Pendulous clusters of small, intensely fragrant cream-colored flowers open in late spring and are one of the most important nectar sources for honeybees in the region, producing a prized light basswood honey, while the large, lopsided heart-shaped leaves cast deep summer shade. Young trees establish well in the dappled light of a ravine understory and gradually push into the canopy as they mature, so a planting site with some high shade is more forgiving than full open sun. Give it deep, humus-rich, consistently moist soil, since this species struggles on compacted or droughty upland ground far more than the oaks and pines it often grows alongside.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto bare, dry, sandy soil in full sun; this Panhandle endemic grows on the longleaf pine sandhills that border steephead ravine rims and needs sharp drainage rather than the moist soil of the ravine floor below.

directions: Narrowleaf false sunflower is a slender, wiry-stemmed perennial restricted to the fire-maintained sandhills of the Florida Panhandle and adjacent southwest Georgia, often growing on the dry upper slopes and rims where steephead ravines cut into longleaf pine uplands. Despite the common name it is not a true sunflower but closely resembles one, producing bright yellow, daisy-like blooms with narrow ray petals from late summer into fall when few other sandhill wildflowers are still flowering. The narrow, almost needle-like leaves and sparse branching give the plant an airy, see-through texture that works well threaded among bunchgrasses in a dry meadow planting. It depends entirely on lean, excessively drained sand and full sun, declining quickly in rich or poorly drained garden soil, and benefits from occasional removal of encroaching woody growth to mimic the periodic fire it would experience in the wild.

planting.note: Direct sow fall-collected seed after 2-3 months of cold, moist stratification into lean, dry, sandy soil in full sun; summer farewell grows in the same sandhill and pine-flatwoods margins that rim Panhandle steephead ravines, never in the shaded ravine itself.

directions: Summer farewell is a low, finely textured subshrub of the pea family found in dry sandhills and open pine flatwoods across the Gulf and Atlantic Coastal Plain, including the sandy uplands that border Apalachicola-region steephead ravines before the ground drops into shaded ravine forest. Its common name comes from the timing of its bloom: dense, rounded heads of small white to cream flowers with dark anthers open from late summer into fall, signaling the season's turn just as many spring and summer wildflowers are finishing. The finely divided, aromatic gray-green foliage releases a resinous scent when brushed and, like other Dalea species, the plant fixes its own nitrogen and needs no fertilizing. Give it full sun and sharp, infertile sand; it is intolerant of rich garden soil or standing water and is best used in a dedicated xeric or sandhill-restoration planting rather than a conventional perennial bed.
